chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Muhammad ibn Sama'ah, from Muhammad ibn Marwan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Indeed, in the wisdom of the progeny of Dawud (peace be upon him): It is befitting for the intellectual Muslim that he is not seen traveling/moving except for three [purposes]: restoration of his livelihood, or provision for his Hereafter, or pleasure in that which is not forbidden.

And it is befitting for the intellectual Muslim that he has an hour in which he devotes himself to his affairs between himself and Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and an hour in which he meets his brethren, with whom he exchanges advice and they exchange advice with him regarding the matters of their Hereafter; and an hour in which he leaves his soul and its pleasures in that which is not forbidden, for indeed these are an aid upon those two hours.

key_terms.حِكْمَةِ آلِ دَاوُدَ: Wisdom of the progeny of Dawud

ai.seo_question: How should a Muslim divide their time according to the wisdom of the progeny of Dawud?
ai.summary: Attributed to Imam al-Sadiq (AS), this hadith codifies the Shia concept of 'al-hal al-thalatha' (the three states), balancing worldly duties, spiritual devotion, and permissible leisure to prevent burnout and moral decay. It reflects the Imams' pragmatic approach to human nature, where rest is not merely idleness but a necessary sustenance for sustained worship and social engagement. This tripartite division underscores the holistic Islamic view of life, integrating material, spiritual, and psychological well-being.
